question: How do you improve incident remediation management processes and separate signal from noise as company scales
answer: There's a threefold aspect to solving this issue. First, there needs to be a technology component where individuals have the ability to record the incidents that happen, understand owners and root cause, and follow progress toward the ultimate solution. Secondly, there needs to be an ownership and accountability piece whereby individuals assigned these task do not view them as lower quality work -- these incidents have to be reported -- but the burden of resolving should be the same order of magnitude as the issue. Finally, there also needs to be a committee of senior leaders who can help ensure that individuals are taking the right level of ownership, creating long-lasting solutions to ensure the issues do not pop up again, as well as understand and opine on larger incident related trends, i.e. see the forest for the trees.

question: The betting questions were quite difficult. One gave two matches, and both the betting odds and the winning odds on each of the two matches. The goal was to allocate 100 dollars between betting on the matches. It was difficult to analyze if I should have put in all my money, or just some of it, as well as if I should all in on the most profitable bet, exposing myself to risk but maximizing EV. The other betting question had a weird betting style, where there were a few things to bet on, and the winner gets a certain proportion of the pot.
answer: I answered them with what was my best guesses. I used the kelly criterion to determine exactly how much money I should put in each option for bets for the first question, but that was strange to me, since it meant that I kept nearly all my money in my pocket, which didn't seem intuitive. The other question, I had no clue, so I just tried my best to maximize EV.

question: Behavior questions are all fine, just the typical ones, but they expect you to present your experiences as much as possible to back up your answers. Technical questions (online tests) involve probability, basic Bayesian theory questions, expected values, strategic betting games, and conditional expected values and probabilities. One example: If the probability of testing positive and negative when having the disease is p1 and p2 respectively. And the probability of having the disease is p3. What is the probability of having the disease if seeing a positive test result?

process: Applied online for Sydney office, 1 online skill test with probability questions, 1 personality test online as well. If you pass that, it will be another similar 1.5-hour interview (this is the final round) with an HR and a senior trader. Interviews are all half behavior and half technical. Typical behavior questions like why trading? why the company? Technical questions are mainly game-based about quick mental math, quick learning, and probability/expected value.

question: Final round case study is on a product that's value is determined by the temperature in Sydney at 12pm a month from now. Some questions they asked:
answer: The product will be most volatile a few hours before the time that the product is settled and least volatile just before the settlement time. This is because information on the temperature is most informative a few hours before (i.e. if the weather is 10 degrees 20 days before the settlement day, this would not greatly affect the predicted temp, but if the weather is 10 degrees on the day of, then it's probably a cold day and will massively affect the predicted temp at 12pm on the settlement day)

question: They gave classic IQ (think Mensa) pattern finding questions, where you would have some sequence of 3 pictures and have to select the fourth iteration of the visual sequence amongst a few options. They would also have this in letters or other symbols. There was also a betting section where you were given a problem space and asked what to bet on / how you would place bets. answer: The IQ questions were just about pattern recognition. Some of them were quite difficult, but the visual ones come with practice. question: The mental math is always so hard, even if you are prepared for it. question: How many cards in a 100 storey tall house of cards?
answer: Top layer has 3 cards, each layer below will have 3 more cards than the layer above it. This forms an arithmetic sequence. So can find that the total is (300+3) * 50 = 15150 cards. But bottom layer doesn’t need to have so many and can actually have 100 less so answer is 15050 cards.

question: Watson likes to challenge Sherlock's math ability. He will provide a starting and ending value describing a range of integers. Sherlock must determine the number of square integers within that range, inclusive of the endpoints.
answer: I tried a brute force approach that coarse-grained searched over the entire space of possible perfect squares within that range, and then zoomed in on the perfect squares that were in the interval range. I also remember using log-transformations to search the space more efficiently, as log grows a lot slower. This was not the right approach however; I do not think I was on the right track either so I would not recommend taking my approach as advice. I did not however received an offer to make the mathematics test due to better suited candidates at the time.

question: Mostly consisted of tests and games. One test to complete sequences (thirty questions), one card game market making simulation (playing against the computer while explaining your decisions to an interviewer sitting with you in the room), one betting card game with two interviewers (just general probability), one verbal and written test (100 verbal questions being played on speaker while completing another 100 written questions at the same time in ten minutes). Then an HR interview and an interview with the head of operations.
answer: Be familiar with market making and the general concept behind it for the market making simulation. You play against "four other players" (CPUs) and you need to make a market over and over while incorporating new information every time a card is flipped. Once you know the basics, be confident to the market you make, rely on your hypothetical average and standard deviation. The sequences test is straightforward so just study up, and the verbal/written test has very basic questions (elementary written math and common knowledge verbal questions).
process: Did one math test, one phone screen with HR (non-technical), one IQ test and then an on-site superday.

question: Technical phone interview had a bunch of components.
answer: Mental math was relatively simple - you could typically simplify them to the product of smaller square roots (i.e. square root 10 * square root 11) so I'd recommend knowing what the square root up to 20 are to help you for this portion.
process: Four step process:

question: There were 3 tests, first was an 8 minute multiple choice maths test, heavy on fractions and decimals. Not overly hard individual questions however very time pressured (80 questions in 8 minutes) with 55 or so required to move on to next test (lower scores may be in 'grey zone' which is allows you to move forward although you are only allowed one of these). Seconds test was sequences where you are to predict the next number in a sequence of numbers by pattern recognition, this is also multiple choice
answer: I'd advise preparing using websites such as trader test this site is actually down however can be accessed through web archives (should be able to find on google). Also when sitting test online, it may be worthwhile to screen capture it to use for future practice of multiple choice format, a lot of time gets spent working out which option corresponds to the answer you put down. For the sequences test the trader test sequences are good, also look out for fraction based sequences where numerator and denominator may need treating separately.
process: Interview process starts with online mental maths test, then is followed by 3 tests in person, HR, technical and assessment day follow

question: Mental math questions (80 of them) - had to complete them in 8 minutes, without a calculator, MCQ. Consisted of + X - /, and would not have been difficult without the extreme time pressure. Afterwards there were 11 math questions to be done in 17 minutes, involving pattern recognition and simple math questions (what is the ratio of cubes painted with two faces to cubes painted on three faces in a 4x5x6 cube painted on the outside).
answer: I practised mental math questions on calculationrankings.com as well as other websites (very easy to Google online), for the math questions, it was simply a matter of going through the calculations calmly and trying to figure out the answer. Some of the pattern recognition questions were absurd - must have guessed correctly. Behavioral questions were standard and easy, and they asked about what you look for in a company, talk about a time you worked on a team, what are the factors that led you to choose trading, why Optiver, etc.
process: First there was a quantitative test, then it was followed by a behavioral interview. Got dinged at this stage

question: Whether I was exclusively applying to finance or if I was applying to be a dev at other companies as well (I have a background in programming and math) . Which other trading companies had I applied to, and how would I decide on a company if I received multiple offers.
answer: Said I was exclusively applying to finance companies which is when she asked me about the ones I was applying to. Listed out about 6 different firms.
process: Was contacted to do a online math test of 80q/8 min and around 11 pattern recognition questions, then had a phone interview with a hr rep

question: The behavioral questions were not so difficult, but rather unexpected. There was no real way to prepare for them, unfortunately. These are not average interview questions and although I felt I did well, I did not make it to the next round after this.
answer: I mostly tried to include details of my life that tried to pertain to the behavioral question.
process: Applied online, responded within one day to set up an online math test. Had roughly 80 questions and sequences. Next round was behavioral. Rejected after that.

question: **Numerical tests:**
answer: **Numerical questions**
process: First stage were three numerical assessments which had to be made in a group at their Amsterdam Office. After each round you had to pass a certain mark to proceed to the next round. Afterwards a phone interview with some personal/behaviour questions and basic questions about trading/market making. Last round a technical interview with two traders and a sitting next to a trader on the desk.

question: They asked you to price an orderbook and play a market making game against CPUs. On the phone, they gave five times each to get to the airport using taxi and train and asked which one you would take. General behavioral questions like why trading, a time you failed, how hard you work, etc. There was also an easy probability game on the sum of two dice. Otherwise it was basic probability, like probability of getting to (2, 2) starting at the origin and going right or up with different probabilities.
answer: For the orderbook, I set the sum of the deviations from the price, weighted by the inverse of the number of orders, equal to 0. I had no idea what I was doing. The market making game I was slow from being too precise with my calculations. The probability game was just making positive EV bets and having a reasonable amount of risk. The airport one was estimating mean and standard deviation and wanting failure to occur with < some probability by approximating as normal and using the 68-95-99.7 rule.
process: Phone call with HR about competitive games and why trading. Phone call with trader about basic probability and standard deviation. Onsite with pattern test, orderbook question, market making and probability game.

question: Most difficult part of early stage is passing mental math test, especially the in person version that is sat after the online version, need to be very quick with a variety of different questions that appear in an unusual format (fill in blank etc). In phone interview wanted to know largest exchange in Europe amongst other standard HR type questions (why Optiver, why trading etc). Wasn’t successful beyond this point but next stage is either interview with trader or final round at offices (have heard of both).
answer: Mental math can be prepared by practicing on various online resources, arithmetic.zetamac being a particular favourite. Only able to sit real test once so definitely worth practicing a lot to make sure are able to comfortably pass. Also look for resources to practice fractions. Largest exchange is I believe eurostoxx. For HR type questions regurgitated various pieces of info from their website. When asked about what other firms I applied to I made sure to list all of their competitors to make clear I had researched.
process: Applied online with Cv and cover, don’t think they were too fussed about contents of cover. Then invited to sit mental math test followed by phone interview

question: Adding and subtracting decimal based mental math was difficult. The sequences test also consisted of some probability questions that required a little bit of out of box thinking. Behavioral phone interview was quite simple but required you to respond quickly and coherently. Probably most difficult that one should study for in behavioral is why this firm?. Do reasearch and network to potentially figure out reasons why you could fit into the firm and develop a story as to why trading would be good for you.
answer: I was unable to successfully answer the probability questions due to me lacking a strong background in probability but looking online afterwards I was able to find solutions. It was mostly conditional probability and one that required knowledge of convergence over large values. For the sequences, some required thinking outside of the box, for example cards as letters or scanning through the alphabet. For behavioral, I went to career fair and talked to a trader who was able to tell me why he worked here and I had similar motivations.
process: Numerical Test, then Phone Interview with HR. Numerical test was mental math and then sequences of numbers. Next was behavioral with basic questions.

question: There were many aspects that were difficult, although I wouldn't say there were too many that were strictly unexpected. Make sure to really drill your mental math components and really know your sequences, and also don't be afraid to use quite a bit of mental math to reach the solution to your sequence problems. These form the crux of the interviewing process and you should not hesitate to dedicate a good few weeks to increasing your sharpness and speed at these topics. Otherwise, focus on logical brainteasers.
answer: I answered the questions rather straightforwardly. There isn't too much complexity or leeway in terms of how they are answered, seeing as they are rather rote mental math or sequence problems. Try to be quick with manipulating large numbers or decimals and seeing the hidden, easier nature of initially daunting number groups. For sequences, just do lots of practice at online websites so that you have the most holistic possible view of the possible varieties of sequences going into the testing environment.
process: Online mental math test followed by lots of sequences. Then a behavioral phone interview with a single technical question.

question: I found the hardest questions to be finding the next number in a series given what seemed like a random sequence of numbers. Another question asked: How many times in a day do the hour hand and the minute hand form a 90 degree angle. Lastly there was a puzzle where I was asked to look at a set of shapes and and symbols and choose an image of the answer that would be the next image in the sequence. During the speed arithmetic part, there were questions asking me to multiply numbers to 4 decimals.
answer: I tried looking for differences and algebraic solutions to find the next number. As for the hour hand question, I put 44. I was able to answer this because I saw it in a question online when I was preparing for the interview. My logic and the answer could be found as follows: in a 12 hour period, the minute hand makes 12 revolutions while the hour hand makes one. If you switch to a rotating coordinate system in which the hour hand stands still, then the minute hand makes only 11 revolutions, and so it is at right angles with the hour hand 22 times. In a 24 hour day you get 2×22=44.
process: I received an online speed arithmetic assessment followed by 8 questions consisting of pattern reading questions and logic and IQ puzzles. Not long after I received an email saying that I had successfully completed the assessment and that I would hear from HR within a week regarding the next recruiting steps. After several weeks I still haven't heard back and assume that I did not do well enough on the initial online assessment to get to the second round.

question: Plenty of application questions that really tested your problem solving skills. Also expect plenty of market simulations and games that test your quantitative skills and probability. Also very important to have a quick math skills, as that will help a lot during later stages of the interview. Very focused interview questions with the real point of seeing if you have the quantitative mindset that will really let you thrive at the firm. After HR interview, not many behavioral questions were really asked.
answer: Quantitative questions are really all about your knowledge about probability and statistics. Definitely be confident about your ability to solve advanced combinatorics and probability questions for trader interviews. HR interview was quite standard and a pretty straightforward process all together. Expect to be thinking quickly on your feet. Also, always be confident about your answer regardless of whatever curveballs that they throw your way. Composure is key as many of the questions are quite difficult.
process: Online application, math test, HR interview, Trader Interview then on-campus final round. Multiple skills tests.

question: Most of the interview onsite consisted of market-making games, which were used to see how quickly you could think on your feet and keep track of multiple pieces of information at once. This was by far the most difficult part of the interview as it was decently math heavy but mostly because I doubt candidates have seen it before. The phone interview had pretty decently easy math questions, though there were questions that dealt heavily in mental math, such as giving the square root of a number and so on
answer: The market making game was pretty difficult for me. The interviewers all seemed pretty uptight and unwilling to reclarify the game, though I assume this is expected behavior. I would recommend knowing the expected values of common things, such as a dice roll, pretty well. Other than that, you are able to see how much "money" you make in these games, though it rarely actually matters (they mostly care about what decisions you make in the process). In the phone interview, they repeatedly will ask you for confidence intervals of your answer
process: I was contacted by Optiver for a numerical assessment, after which there was one phone interview. After that, I was flown out for an onsite interview

question: The HR phone interview questions were (not inclusive, and not in order):
answer: In the same order as above:
process: You apply online with a letter and your CV. If they like what they see, you can continue to the numerical test which is described already quite accurately by many people before me. Following this there is a HR phone interview where they gauge your motivation and interest. The last round consists of a slightly longer HR interview with some behavioral questions, followed by a technical interview, and finally followed by a desk chat with a trader, where you can ask some questions and will also be asked some questions.

question: The initial mental math test was fairly challenging and a bit unprecedented. It consisted of a combination of mental math and sequencing questions with the aim of maximising the number of correctly answered questions in a set time. There is a combination of straightforward maths and difficult math questions and the sequences are not the most obvious and can be geometric/linear. An example of a comparable question can be 99x44 with the aim of calculating it in your head. Later rounds can have probability questions based on coin flips values.
answer: Practice is quite crucial for mental math so it become sort of like muscle memory to do the calculations quickly. This is applicable for the sequences as well so that you get exposed to multiple different types of sequences and know what possible options to look for when faced with a new sequence. The personality questions cannot really be prepared for as it is an intrinsic and inherent quality so try to be yourself. Also practice some questions on things like coin flips to know the basics of it.
process: The interview process was quick and smooth. After the initial online application the rest of the stages progressed quickly.

question: There weren't really any difficult or unexpected interview questions, they were mainly very simple and common behavioral. E.g. Why did you apply to Optiver, why do you want to do trading, why did you major in the major that you did, why did you choose your college, a brief resume overview, and small questions based off of these. I don't think they cared much about the behavioral portion, as most people passed, who I know. Should be similar to similar prop trading places nearby and nothing new or difficult.
answer: I answered the former by saying that they had a really good intern program, and that they were very good at what they do: options. I majored in the major that I did because I really enjoyed this honors class that I chose first quarter where I really pushed myself. College: also that I wanted to challenge myself and I liked the atmosphere of intellectual stimulation, and the resume portion is basically: Tell me about yourself, where I ran them through my resume and what I do in college at the moment.
process: I first completed the online test, which was essentially speed math. After that, I moved on to the behavioral, which was easy, but I messed up.

question: The hardest type of questions had to do with the fractions. 56 / 7 / x = 4. Then you had to solve for x in a matter of seconds.
answer: To solve these mental math questions fast. You need to practice, practice, practice. There is no way around it. Just muscle memory. For the decimal multiplication just think of it in terms of percentages. So for 0.008 * x = 0.00056.... we see that 0.00056 is just 7% of 0.008 which is 0.07. Don't psych yourself out with all the zeroes.
process: Applied online. Then received a numerical test. 80 questions in 8 minutes. Not too hard. Simple mental math. If you practice you should do just fine. Need around 55 to pass. Then another test with some probability and sequences. Nothing too unexpected.

question: Fermi Questions: Approximately how many ping pong balls does it take to fill up the Empire State Building (in New York City)?
answer: First one: Just build up volumetrically using orders of magnitdues estimates. For example start off with an approximation for the diamete rof a ball and then keep working your way up. Now esimate the number of floors of the building and the total square footagge of each floor and height, and take the appropriate division
process: First round: Online iq test and numerical literacy test

question: Coding interview questions - one was to find the number of days between two given dates. The dates were given in a string format so they had to be parsed properly to be workable. Another question was to find the whether adjacent tiles in a 2D matrix of integer values summed to a given target number. The HR questions were your standard behavioural questions with no technical knowledge required. Mostly walking through job experiences on your CV as well as a few questions about what subjects you enjoyed most/least.
answer: There are a number of ways to do the coding questions with no one answer. Parsing the date from a string to an integer and then calculating respective differences between year, month, day components of the date and then accounting for leap year constraints. The matrix sum question was most easily solved by using classic graph traversal methods like DFS or BFS (DFS probably the easiest to implement). The HR questions were pretty standard and if you have adequate material prepared and some good off the cuff experiences then you should have no issues.
process: 3hr programming test on HackerRank and a phone interview with HR. Coding test was not too bad, questions very much doable and not a whole lot of time pressure.

question: The most difficult questions were definitely the brain teaser questions. There's a reason that they're called brain teasers! With that being said, from everything that I've heard and my experience, it didn't seem necessary to get the right answer as long as you were able to explain your though process in depth. So my advice would be to learn how to "think out loud" during these types of interviews because that is what the firm is looking for. They want smart people who are exceptional communicators.
answer: I answered these questions to the best of my ability but I found that I was wrong on nearly all of them. Many of them have very long and arithmetic intensive answers and then they also have a short nice trick that makes the problem quite simple. I would of course choose the very long method because of the time restriction and pressure that made it tough to process and think of a strategic method. I would definitely recommend to try to stay as relaxed as possible because the more you freak yourself out, the less your going to be able to think.
process: I was sent an online math test. After I passed that, I had to take a video test and personality test. From there, I had a phone interview with a trader.

question: It wasn't a technical question, but more of a question that was difficult for me to answer as I am still uncertain about my future. I don't remember exactly word to word but it sounded something like ->
answer: The personality test was probably the test that I was least prepared for, so my first answers were not really honest. I would just deliver simple and short answers, in a very short time frame as if I had the answers prepared ahead of time. Then the recruiters have noticed this and started to ask more details and here I started to slow with my answers. As for the quantitative problem, I could not solve it as it required too much time for me to solve, I know only that it involved Bayesian Statistics, so you had to make a tree-diagram and the ranking of the players would change after every game.
process: This was my first interview so I don't know exactly how it was as I don't have anything to compare it with, but overall it consisted of an arithmetic test of 80 questions in 8 minutes. Then there was a personality test in which I had to talk with recruiters. The third part consisted of probability and logic problems. I am still waiting for the next stage in my interviewing process. The math rounds were great for me as this is related to my are of study but I think I failed my personality test, I had several awkward silence moments and couldn't give simple answer to some personal questions.

question: I would definitely say that the most difficult interview questions were the math problems in the third stage of the interview process, where the traders asked me math questions that covered market sizing, finding square roots of large non-perfect squares, and AIME-like questions. The problems weren't difficult if you could find the trick to solve them, but the problem is that these questions were specifically designed to trip people up to see if you could stand under pressure and perform well at the same time.
answer: For the first round, I went on rankyourbrain.com and took the mental math test on expert level a few times. I believe I passed the first round relatively soundly. The second round's behavioral I just thought about why I wanted to join Optiver and why trading interested me. For the third round, I looked at past Optiver questions on Glassdoor and WSO and made sure I could do all of them. After I completed those questions, I completed some past AIME questions that you can find online for free. Overall, the interview process definitely requires a lot of preparation.
process: The interview was a four part process. The first part was an online, 80-question, 8-minute mental math test. The second part was a behavioral test that involved speaking with a recruiter about my interest in trading and Optiver. The third part was a quantitative technical test with two traders who asked me mental brain teasers and difficult math problems.

question: As I mentioned, there were 80 questions in 8 minutes. These consisted of decimal and fractional multiplication, division, addition and subtraction. Each question attempted gave +1 while each question wrong gave an additional -2 (overall -1). For example, if you attempted 60Qs and got 5 wrong, your score was 60 - 2*5 = 50. The pass mark was 50 which I think was fairly challenging without significant practise. The sequences test had a different scoring system. +1 for correct answer -1 for incorrect, 0 if skipped.
answer: I answered the questions using the mental math I had studied at rankyourbrain. They were simple questions, however it was the time pressure that was challenging. Sometimes the order the question was presented in was difficult. For example 1/3 * ___ = 1/2. The answer is obviously 3/2 however you had to select a multiple choice box, which might say 9/4. Quite annoying really. Other examples of questions were 0.031 - 0.007, 9.1*43, etc. etc. An example of a sequence question would be 2, 3, 1, 4, 0 and you had to select the correct next answer (5)
process: Was invited to take the Optiver 80 questions in 8 minutes test and a sequences test (26 questions in 30 minutes). Both were quite challenging and I would advise using a site such as rankyoubrain to study. Surprisingly the tests were on paper and multiple choice.

question: Three behaviour questions.
answer: Q1: from my point of view, this question is not very difficult to answer since very hard to get the working permit in Switzerland for Non-EU citizens and my girlfriend wants to go back to work making the convincing reasons.
process: The first round consists of a numerical test (80 mental math problems in 8 mins) and a logical reasoning test(30 problems in 19 minutes) all online. Two days after that, HR called you that the HR behaviour interview was arranged on next Monday.

question: Asked a lot of math questions, only the HR interview had many behavioral questions. The math questions mostly related to probability and other applied topics that can be learned in undergraduate courses. There was a lot of focus on outside of the box thinking rather than straight computation. These quesiton can be found in books like Heard on the Street, 150 most frequently asked questions in quantitative finance interviews, etc. Doing those books will get you to the finish line at least for the phone interview.
answer: The questions I was asked can be found in books like Heard on the Street, 150 most frequently asked questions in quantitative finance interviews, etc. Doing those books will get you to the finish line at least for the phone interview. For brainteasers look up famous puzzles book on the internet. The arithmetic test was the most stressful hurdle because people don't usually practice it. Find a test online and practice doing basic operations to two decimal places in your head, accurately. A score of 50/80 or more should pass you.
process: Call with HR first, then arithmetic test, then phone interview with trader, then onsite. Pretty transparent about the process.

question: Few easy multiple-option type questions, followed by also not so complex algorithm and data structures. Last question is the most difficult, requires knowledge of data structures, but also important how would you design the solution, how would you optimally solve the problem, validate the input/output. Everything is tested automatically, and there are few sample test cases included, so you don't have to think too much on testing it on your local environment. You can simply run it through hackerranks.
answer: Know what is an abstract modifier and what effect it has on the class.
process: A very general get to know phone call, explaining the process.

question: Make a market on a dynamic card game. You are given a standard deck of cards and asked to find the expected value of 10 cards. Next they give you two cards and tell you that you are playing against two other (simulated) players. After each card is flipped you have to adjust your market based on the change in expected value of the sum of 10 cards. At the end, they ask you how you think you did, what the total sum is, and how much money you made. Overall, very challenging in the moment, but looking back on it, wasn't too bad.
answer: You are given a standard deck of cards and asked to find the expected value of 10 cards. Next they give you two cards and tell you that you are playing against two other (simulated) players. After each card is flipped you have to adjust your market based on the change in expected value of the sum of 10 cards. At the end, they ask you how you think you did, what the total sum is, and how much money you made. Overall, very challenging in the moment, but looking back on it, wasn't too bad. I didn't get an offer
process: Interview was challenging. Started by taking three tests: one math, one sequences, and one multitasking. 1-1 interview was conducted by a senior trader during lunch. Ended with a market making simulation and a gambling game.

question: I have had multiple questions in the IQ test where you need to logical reasoning. This is called syllogismn and annologismn. You can train this by drawing ven diagrams. Further more you need to have a clear view on the business core business. HFQ trading, market making, liquidity providing. Your English needs to be near native and also during the interviews they test your math skills in various ways. Be prepared on situations where they will distract you from the questions they are asking. In the end you should be very enthousiast about trading.
answer: All questions should be answered without guesing. I is way better to say that you do not know the answer than guessing. This is ofcourse the same in trading. It is better to not trade than to make a wrong trade in essence. Also you should not be scared to make faults. Being secure in and show confidence is a major asset where they are looking for. If you have any experience in trading it is a major edge. In the end it is just a game of which anyone can learn if you are motivated. Try to not show scareness
process: First you need to do a math test. This is fairly dueable if you train for it. Next there is an IQ test. Than HR interview and finanlly a case study. Math questions range from 0.1*14 to 1882+9977. No fractions.

question: A technical question in the final round about a tournament where you had to identify risk-free arbitrage opportunities. There are basically 4 groups of 4 teams. And they progress through a knock-out style tournament that goes on to quarter-finals, semi-finals, and finals. Each stage has a pay-out and each team has a price you can buy them for. You have to identify opportunities where you can lock in a profit with 100% certainty. Basically if a team gets $100 for getting through to the quarter finals, and you could buy an entire group of 4 for less than $200 (because 2 teams from each group go through to quarter finals), then that is a risk-free arbitrage opportunity. I completely stuffed up this question, you get 5 minutes to read the question and it is worded very confusingly. I just didn't get it in the moment, but it is actually not so hard given time to think about it.
answer: I answered the question very poorly because i didn't understand it at the time. Basically, if a team gets $x for getting to the quarter finals, then you know that for every group of 4 teams at least 2 of them goes through to the quarter finals. So if you can buy an entire group for less than $2x, then you have a risk free arbitrage opportunity because 2 teams will definitely go through from each group. Then, you can start looking at buying 2 groups of 4 teams together, because you know that 4 of the 8 teams will go through to quarter finals and then 2 of those will go through to semi-finals. So then there is another pay-out for semi-finals. So you just have to calculate whether you can buy them with a risk-free opportunity or not.
process: - Started with online math speed test. 80 questions in 8 minutes. Simple additions, subtractions, divisions and multiplications. Some fractions included, need to be able to flip fractions around quickly in your head and work with them. Multiplications fairly easy, the hardest might be 23 x 16 or something like that (from memory).

question: The hard questions begin from the in person interview. The technical aspect involved doing answering numerous probability/EV based questions based on card games. One example question involved calculating the expected value of a card drawn from a deck of 52 cards (J = 11, etc.), which was quite easy. Then they asked to calculate the expected value if the value of spades doubled, which requires you to think a little bit.
answer: The expected value of the first problem is 7, then once a suit is doubled the expected value is (5/4)*7 = 8.75. In terms of the technical interview on the assessment day, I struggled because of the information I needed to process. The way to succeed was to look at minimum/maximum payouts from buying/selling a bunch of teams - you had to consider the cost of a whole group of teams. For example, buying a whole group of teams might have cost $180 when the guaranteed payout would be at least $200, which is an arbitrage. Or selling a group of teams would be $260 when in the worst case scenario you would have to payout $250.
process: Did a maths and sequences test on campus which was relatively easy. Then followed be HR screening and then an in person interview with a trader. I passed that and was invited to Sydney for an assessment day, which I did not pass.

question: First round was an in house numerical test, first was 8 minutes 80 questions on simple arithmetic, passing mark was 56 with negative marking for wrong or skipped questions. Second test was 30 questions on sequences with no negative marking and 30 minutes to complete, one of the questions had 3 answers that were the same value but the representation (reduced fraction, non-reduced fraction, power) was part of the sequence pattern; pass was 23. Final test was 40 mixed questions (from both previous types) and a few questions asking about unit of time calculations (Xdays Yhours Zminutes - Tdays Uhours Vminutes). Pass was 25, negatively marked again.
answer: Did not prepare for the financial news questions as wasn't aware this was part of the test, however was able to answer reasonably. In short describe a recent event (Italian election result) and theorize what impact the result may have on European markets (higher % for fringe parties, unpredictable future etc).
process: First round - numerical / arithmetic testing

question: There was nothing particularly difficult; be sure to expect timed mental math questions with follow up questions on how sure you are. Questions went over basic statistics and probabilities, sometimes it was hard to follow just because of how the question was worded. I.e. What is the square root of 30 to the nearest two decimal points? How sure are you?, You are on the bottom left corner of a two by two square. How many different ways can you get to the top right corner if you cannot go backward?
answer: Answering the questions required basic factorization, using z-score and other statistical concepts, thinking quickly. The math was on par with basic Mathcounts / AMC level math questions. Other than that, trader was fairly reasonable when it came to communicating and providing hints of necessary. Highly recommend that you review brainteaser guidebooks prior to interviewing for the technical. They'll double check on superday to make sure you weren't cheating, so not much point in doing so. Good luck.
process: The interview process consisted of 1 mental math assessment, a phone screen, a personality test, a technical interview, and superday after that.

question: The mental math test was 80 questions in 8 minutes, it was quite difficult. Tradertest or zetamac are two websites that would suffice in preparing one for the test. Then the phone interview was a mix of fit questions and difficult probability questions, asked in increasingly difficult order. They were centered around games and the questions were targeted at expected value. I made a few mistakes on 2/5 questions and was eliminated after this round. Any undergraduate probability course would suffice to prepare for this.
answer: I practiced mental math out loud to prepare for the mental math test, which was online. I used a book call Secrets of Mental Math. For probability, I used books like Heard on the Street to prepare, as well as probability cheat sheets online as a reference. The questions were all variations on well known problems, nothing crazy. It would be good to take a look at expected value sections of a probability textbook and various identities for variance and how to minimize variance while maximizing expectation.
process: The interview process consists of a targeted email, then a mental math test, then a phone call with a trader.

question: In the second phone interview the questions were all probability based. question: He asked me a simple expected value of a game which was easy enough. From there the trader took me through different scenarios of the game, such as what if you get a second chance, what if your get a third chance, and thus what would be the expected value of the game. He additionally asked me if you had one chance to play the game how much would you bet on the game, if you had a thousand chances to play how much would you bet on the game, and finally he asked me a probability question that was unrelated to the game, but he asked for a confidence interval.
answer: For the expected value, I simply used the summation rule where you take the largest number, let's say n, and multiply it by n+1 and then divide by 2 to get the total, and then divide by n again to get the expected value. For a scenario in which you play only once, the variance of the game is much higher so you want to be more conservative with how much you want to pay, so a bit less than the expected value. For larger samples of the games, you can bet closer to the expected value. For expected value of repeated tries, I wasn't sure but it is definitely more than the expected value.

He decides to use them as taste testers to determine which bottle of wine contains the poison. The poison when taken has no effect on the prisoner until exactly 24 hours later when the infected prisoner suddenly dies. The King needs to determine which bottle of wine is poisoned by tomorrow so that the festivities can continue as planned. Hence he only has time for one round of testing. How can the King administer the wine to the prisoners to ensure that 24 hours from now he is guaranteed to have found the poisoned wine bottle?

question: 1.You and your opponent flip a coin. If the first player gets heads, the second player pays him $30. If he flips tails, the coin goes to the second player. If the second player flips heads, he wins $30 from the first player. How much should you pay to go first?
answer: 1. The answer is $10 assuming the game goes on until someone wins (because that's what makes the problem interesting anyway). Let event A be defined as "Player who went first wins" and event B be defined as "Player who went second wins" Now: P(A) = 1/2 + 1/2^3 + 1/2^5 + ... P(B) = 1/2^2 + 1/2^4 + 1/2^6 + ... Notice that the Probability of A occurring is twice that of B occurring in this sequence. We know that these two events span the sample space (we assume one will eventually win), therefore we can apply a tenet of probability: P(A) + P(B) = 1 Since A is twice as likely as B of occurring: P(A) = 2P(B); substitute into the above equation. 1 = 3P(B); P(B) = 1/3, and thus, P(A) = 2/3 Now expected value for whomever goes first is: E(V) = (2/3)($30) + (1/3)(-$30) = $10 Let x be the amount you pay to go first. As long as x < $10, you are making a good deal.

question: You observe a symmetric random walk starting at zero. You are allowed to stop at any time, and your payoff when you stop is the position of the walk minus a cost that accumulates with each step. What stopping strategy maximizes your expected payoff?
answer: I explained that because the walk has no upward drift, simply waiting is not beneficial; the longer you wait, the more you pay in running costs. At the same time, the variance of the walk creates occasional positive spikes. So the only rational approach is to stop when the walk reaches a sufficiently positive level that compensates for the cost of waiting. I said the optimal strategy is a threshold rule: once the walk rises above a certain positive boundary, you lock in the gain. I also added that the boundary depends on how expensive waiting is—higher cost means you stop earlier. The interviewer mainly wanted to see whether I understood that optionality must outweigh running cost, and that the solution is not “wait forever” or “stop immediately,” but a balance between risk and cost.

question: Walk me through a DCF.
answer: Project unlevered free cash flows over five to ten years starting from EBIT, tax it to NOPAT, add back D&A, subtract capex and the change in net working capital, calculate a terminal value using perpetuity growth or an exit multiple, discount everything back at WACC, sum to enterprise value, subtract net debt, and divide by diluted shares for implied share price, always sensitizing the output since terminal value drives most of it, net income flows from the income statement to the top of the cash flow statement and into retained earnings, non-cash charges like D&A and stock comp get added back, working capital changes and investing and financing activities follow, and the resulting change in cash hits the balance sheet cash line, which is the plug that makes it balance, and for the fit question the answer that works is specific rather than aspirational — name why you tested the interest, cite two actual deals the firm advised on in your sector, and reference real networking conversations, because interviewers hear the same rehearsed four sentences all day and the only differentiator is evidence you did work nobody required.
process: I submitted my application in early spring, more than a year before the internship actually started — Goldman's timeline has crept absurdly early, and by the time most people hear the process has opened, the best groups are already deep in it. The online form itself took about two hours: resume, transcript, a division preference ranking, and a handful of short written responses about why banking and why Goldman, which I rewrote four times and had two upperclassmen tear apart. About three weeks later I got the HireVue link — an asynchronous video interview where you get a question on screen, roughly thirty seconds to think, and two minutes to record an answer with no retakes. The questions were almost entirely behavioral ("tell me about a time you worked on a team under pressure," "walk me through your resume," "why this division"), and the strangest part was talking into a webcam with no human on the other end; I practiced with a friend on Zoom for a week beforehand just to get used to it. Then silence for about five weeks, which is the part nobody warns you about — I assumed I'd been rejected and started applying elsewhere. The superday invitation came by email with about ten days' notice: four interviews, thirty minutes each, back to back, with a mix of analysts, VPs, and one MD. The junior interviewers went hardest on technicals — walk me through a DCF, how do the three statements link, what happens to free cash flow if depreciation increases by ten dollars, why would two comparable companies trade at different multiples — and the senior ones barely touched them and instead pushed on fit, deal interest, and whether I actually understood what the job looked like day to day. I'd drilled the standard technical guides until I could answer the common ones cold, which mattered less for being impressive than for freeing up attention to actually hold a conversation. The offer call came eight days later from HR, with a verbal exploding deadline of about a week, and the written package followed the next morning.

question: Walk me through an amortization schedule for a mortgage.
answer: An amortization schedule just shows how each monthly payment gets split between interest and principal until the loan hits zero. The interest piece is last month's balance times the monthly rate, so the annual rate divided by 12, and whatever's left of the payment goes to knocking down principal. The payment is set at close so the loan pays off exactly at the end of the term. Early on the balance is big, so almost the whole payment is interest and barely any touches principal and then more goes to principal over the life of the loan. I kept it as simple as I could because I feel that shows you truly understand it.

process: I applied online through their website. later i got a hirevue. I completed that and was alerted via emial about a superday.

question: Most difficult was "Tell me about a time you had to make a quick decision", it caught me off guard. Also got asked about something new I learned about markets in the past 6 months, tell me about a time that you made a mistake, tell me about a time that you ran into a problem when working in a team. The first question they asked me was walk me through your resume, and I think I spent too long talking about that. Overall the questions weren't too bad but I blanked on that first one about the quick decision.
answer: Quick decision I talked about fielding a client call in a club that I'm in at school, the client was very unhappy and demanded a refund that we couldn't give. I had to make the quick decision to reject the client from our organization even though we lost the money. process: I applied online on their website and received an email asking to complete a Hirevue video-recorded interview.

question: The questions weren't difficult. I don't think I was surprised by any of them. Maybe I didn't expect that they will ask me to walk them through my resume. I thought that this question is mostly asked during a superday, not in an on-demand interview but somehow this was the first question I had. I had only 2 minutes to answer so I almost run out of time. Another small difficulty was that I felt that I didn't have enough time to answer some of the questions. I had 30 seconds to prepare and 2 minutes to answer. I feel that giving 2,5 or 3 minutes would be a better idea. Other questions were pretty basic, like why do you want to work in this company etc.
answer: I did my research so whenever I was answering questions related to the company, I tried to say what I learned from other employees or their website. Definitely do your research and have your answer ready. When I was walking them through my resume, I tried to mention information that are the most essential and that would help me prove that I have all the skills they are looking for. Other than that I tried to be confident, speak clearly and not too fast. The fact that you have a limited time might be scary, but it's important to stay calm and confident in your abilities.
process: Applied through the official website and through school career service website. I applied for 3 different positions. Before submitting my application I didn't network as much as I should. However, I received my first round interview after 2 weeks, which was HireHue. I had 8 questions, they were pretty straightforward, mostly behavioral.

question: 1+2+...+100=? (no calculators allowed)
answer: I knew that 1+...+n=n(n+1)/2 so just plugging n=100 gives 1+2+...+100=100*101/2=5,050. I suspect if you don't know that formula you could have seen that by trying for n=1,2,3,... and observing they're all n(n+1)/2.
process: Applied start of September, was invited to the virtual interview mid-October and then was invited to a superday in London mid-November for 3 back to back 1-1 interviews.

question: They didnt as anything overly difficult or unexpected. The key thing is to be prepared and know the role you are interviewing for so that you can prepare for it will by studying and being aware of what is going on in the markets at the time of the interview. Know your resume well and be able to articulate any weaknesses in your experience or in yourself for that matter. Those are the key take aways from the interview experience. also ve able to speak about outside interests if they ask you about any
answer: I answered the questions based on resources i've found on wso and online. The key is to really know why you want to go in to the specific field and what your "story" is. process: they want intelligent and passionate people, so you need to network and show them that as with all finance jobs

question: There wasn't anything too out of the ordinary, mainly behavioral questions. The first two were about working within teams and facing difficult situations. The remaining three corresponded to the roles that I chose, why I wanted to pursue them/why I was a good fit. Just screwed up by not going into the Hirevue 100% prepared and stumbling over a few answers. Was also thrown off by addressing all three divisions within one Hirevue. It is also just never not awkward talking to a screen, so they aren't my favorite.
answer: Gave examples of teamwork through involvement with extracurriculars at school, talked about my go-to failure (failing a class that was supposed to be easy, going to office hours and fixing that). I had networked a bit with people from the firm in the different divisions that I applied to, which were securities, global investment research, and risk. Knew some associates at the firm who were alum at my school and attended the Beyond the Classroom event focusing in risk, so could speak knowledgeably to those two.
process: Submitted 3 applications online through their applicant portal, completed a Hirevue about 2 weeks later.

question: I didn't get asked anything too difficult. I think the most challenging question I got was tell me about a time you had to meet a deadline, and then I just kept talking about my resume from there. I got asked how I see myself in the division and how I think it works, but that was pretty easy. I talked about the groups/desks I was most interested in and a small reason why. I think if you just approach it as a normal interview for a company it'll go fine. Make sure you know who leads the group/who is the global head because that makes everything easier.
answer: I talked about my resume in detail, and told it like a story. I wanted to explore X, so I did Y. When Y went well I also tried Z but didn't like it as much. On top of that I also talked about how my interests matched the position and how I liked more fast paced environments and how that would apply to S&T. I talked about specific desks and products I thought were the most interesting, and who I've talked to so far in S&T that have helped me understand more. It's also important to have a good elevator pitch of why you're there.
process: GS Sec Div Superday was 3 one on one interviews with associates and higher. Each asked two situational (not behavioral) questions that were super easy to answer. Then we talked about my resume and I just ended up asking a lot of questions. Not one technical question at all; I think they just wanted someone who wasn't too boring and could talk the talk.

question: Most difficult question asked were about my future plan for higher education, it took some time to convince them that I don't have any plans for higher education for the next 2-3 years. I was asked this question nearly at each round of interviews telephonic and in person.
answer: I answered saying the question regarding higher education saying I'm currently simultaneous pursuing the CFA program and have two more levels to go. My application with two years of work experience at Goldman would look great for my application, and only within two years time period would I be able to make an impact where I can ask an MD for a recommendation for my application.
process: Process lasted over 5-6 months, beginning with multiple telephonic rounds (3 rounds with Bengalore team, 3 rounds with regional teams HK,LDN,NY). Finally was called in for a Super day along with 8 candidates. Had 4-5 rounds with multiple VPs and Analyst. Questions of Product knowledge, previous work ex, puzzles were asked. Why GS, Why leaving the current role was asked as well.

question: The questions weren't difficult so much as unexpected on the whole. I was prepared to answer technicals but what was asked were more general scenarios and how I would go about considering a situation or addressing a given incident. Was told the interview was standardized for the first time so this may be why. Hardest question was probably asking me to talk about something I was passionate about because the follow-ups got very granular (i.e. when I spoke about a part of my major I was asked to detail what my plans were for my senior thesis experiment).
answer: I spoke about my major in pretty significant depth as the thing I was passionate about, and when asked about my senior thesis I was upfront and said I was not yet at that point, but I spoke about a bunch of research and potential avenues I could explore. I think the idea was just to show you were intellectually curious and passionate about something and could go in depth on that thing and show you put in deep thought and analysis. Again, wasn't a hard question so much as a tough follow-up.
process: Applied online, received a single hirevue for all divisions I applied to, invited to superday which was 2x 1:1 and 1x 2:1. More fit/thought process than technical.

question: How would you price an insurance? I was helped by looking at it from a purely probability problem.
answer: Pricing an insurance is based on the expectation of the losses. An insurer will ask a premium on top of the expected loss which is possible because an insurance buyer is generally risk averse and will therefore be willing to pay a premium to hedge his risk.
process: First application online. Mostly based on resume and motivation. Video interview with five situations. Given 2 minutes to answer them. Mostly behavioral. Final round 3 x 30 min interview with seniors. More in-depth, finance related.

process: Was recruited off of LinkedIn by a newer 'experienced recruiter'. Began with a phone interview that took about 25minutes. Very basic behavior/fit questions and basically a "tell me about yourself."

question: Some of the technicals were tough but also they were what you would expect in an investment banking interview. I got asked to "walk me through an LBO model", got asked various accounting questions, and other questions that were tough but expected. Nothing felt unfairly difficult, however. Besides that, there were a few unexpected brain teasers I got asked that were a little tough. For example, I got asked "What does the U.S. spend in haricuts per year?" and other random brainteasers like that, but these questions were more for fun and to see how my though process works.
answer: For the accounting problems, I simply walked through the balance statements. For example, if depreciation goes up by ten, then you know that before tax income goes down by ten on the income statement but net income only goes down by 6 (if 40% tax rate). On the cash flow statement, cash flows go up 4. Finally, on the balance sheet, retained earnings go down 6 and on the other side assets decrease 10 but cash goes up 4 to balance it. Regarding the brain teasers, I simply walked through the problem by guessing how much the average person spends on a haircut times the average times a person goes per year times the number of people in the U.S.
process: Very easy, relaxed process. I had a phone interview and then a super day. Both of which were mostly conversational and not overly intense. Still, you should know your technicals and be prepared for a few hard questions.

question: Interview was for the securities team. Unlike other places they did not ask for a stock pitch or ask any behavioural questions. All of the questions were brain teasers. For example, how far is the sun from pluto? Several questions on probability and expected value for a dice game. Follow up questions on the dice game if certain conditions were changed. How many swimming pool are there in Australia? Finding a fake coin using a scale.
answer: Interview was for the securities team. Unlike other places they did not ask for a stock pitch or ask any behavioural questions. All of the questions were brain teasers. For the probability questions you had to be really solid at maths, it was expected that you could do the maths in your head quickly. For the swimming pool question you could predict how many people one swimming pool served and then used the population to find total number. Got stumped on the coding question, didn't have a solid background in coding so they sort of skipped it.

process: Did online HireVue. After about a month got an email from the recruiter that I was invited to Superday. Superday consisted of 3 back to back 30 min interviews.

question: 1. How can you approximate the swap rate, knowing only the forward rates prevailing at the moment for several maturities? Please explain the process in detail, i.e. bootstrapping, fundamental links, etc.
answer: 1. Explain how to bootstrap the yield curve in detail. Rough concept can be found here https://financetrain.com/bootstrapping-spot-rate-curve-zero-curve/. However highly recommend to invest the time to read Hull for more details and intuitive understanding of it. After, use the swap formula to come up with the estimate. Always highlight what kind of approximation you used (i.e. linear, etc) to the interviewer.
process: the interview process was great, but I feel a bit more structure would be very useful: I was interviewed by more than 10+ people from various departments and had to come to the office 5+ times. In my case it was not as easy since I was working full time in local IB

question: Unexpected prop trading types of questions such as probability and expected value on dice, poker, coin and so on. I was not really expecting this type of questions on sell-side sales and trading role but interviewer asked a lot of these questions (possibly because he is from the strats team) Other than that it was standard sales and trading behavioural and technical questions such as why trading, tell me a time you worked well in a team and so on. Generally I felt that it was harder than other BB interviews I have done.
answer: Probabilty and expected value questions were answered using basic probability theories to calculate the percentage of pnl and so on. The key is to say out your thought process in front of the interviewer as it is important to let interviewer know your thought process as this is more important than getting the right answer. The interviewer would try to pressurise the candidate so it is important to stay calm and try to solve the problems as quickly as possible. Other behavioural questions were answered based on my experience.
process: Initial video interview followed by a few rounds of one on one face interview. Interview was a good mixture of technical and behavioural questions

role: Goldman Sachs Sales and Trading Summer Analyst
question: The questions were essentially all behavioral and situational. I was surprised that there were no technical finance questions but I could see that the questions were there to test your ability to think strategically. One of the most difficult questions was the strategy I employed when I was working with individuals who had intentions that were in direct contrasts to mine. This is essentially a situational question that tested your ability to manage relationships which makes since given the client driven nature of the work.
answer: The key is being concise and laying out a clear structure for the answer. For me, a gave an overview of where I got that experience from. Then I would present my solution to the problem by starting off by presenting the parties at hand. After I would go over the agendas of the various parties and how they worked against each other. I addressed the political ramifications of each agendas and talked about the end goals of each group and how I was able to navigate through those to merge it in a compromising way. The key in this is to describe your ability to communicate and understand expectations of other people.
process: I attended the info session for the sales and trading group at my university in the Spring. I set up multiple coffee chats with the people in attendance at the event. One of them asked me for my resume. Roughly a week later, a recruiter reached out to me and asked if I could attend a super day roughly a week after finals ended.

question: Asked me about my Phd for the warm up and directly went into questioning me. Two mathematical questions and one coding questions.
answer: i, fourth moment of a Gaussian distribution - it was expected that I did all on paper and took him with me. I just mentioned integration by parts and tried to do the calculation. Having not done it for a long time I came to a wrong solution and said that this is too much calculation to do. Additionally you need to be aware of a coordinate transformation from cartesian to polar coordinates.
process: I applied online before August and got the interview in october. Recruiter did contacted me and scheduled an interview.

question: Can you tell me about a time you worked on a team?
answer: In general, to prep for S&T interviews you need to know what is happening in the markets, make sure to read the WSJ, Bloomberg, FT, or the Economist everyday, have a story that makes sense, know your mental math and brainteasers, and have examples of times where you have shown qualities that all the banks look for: leadership, teamwork, work ethic, time management skills, etc....
process: The hiring process was straight forward. I did a HireVue, then flown to NY for a superday. Afterwards, I was notified the day after I got the offer.

question: The most difficult questions entailed solving various probability and mathematics problems, in addition to coding algorithms, both verbally, on paper, and via HackerRank/CoderPad. They really only seemed to care about my problem solving approach and how well I was able to explain my thought process. Little if any emphasis was placed on my ability to converse with the interviewer and maintain a genial conversation. This is probably understandable as Strats is a very results-driven division, and the interview process reflects this characteristic.
answer: I attempted to walk the interviewer through questions that I was not fully able to answer from the get-go. For instance, one of the questions had me compute the estimated score that one would get by playing a card game with 3 black and 3 red cards. Each draw of a black card results in 1 being added to your score, and each draw of a red card results in 1 being subtracted from your score. I was to estimate the expected score one would receive from playing this game, assuming I would leave the game at the most opportune time.
process: The interview process began with an online HackerRank test, followed by 3 phone interviews, and then by an in-person superday.

question: My background is in equities and the position was in credit and fixed income. As a result I didn't do so well as I haven't looked at bonds and CDS for a long time. answer: I didn't do well at all. I think I managed to get to the end of the answers with a lot of help of the interviewer who was very nice. It was rather embarrassing because I had to remind myself of bonds and yields but I think he understood I hadn't looked it it for a few years.
process: I got the interview via a recruiter. It was just an initial telephone interview lasting about 45 minutes.

question: Was interviewing for securities and was asked a question about cash flows. answer: I answered very calmly to the question about academic integrity. process: The hiring process was pretty simple. I spoke to a recruiter in that division during a coffee chat. applied a few days after then was selected for an online interview. I did bad cause it was very weird but still got invited to the super day.

question: The most difficult interview question entailed finding the expected value of a deck with 3 +1 cards and 3 -1 cards, assuming drawing is done at random until the optimal time to leave the game occurs.
answer: With the deck question, I simply simulated the different cases and ended up guessing a value between 0 and 3, being that 0 is the minimum value for the worst case (drawing 3 -1 and 3 +1) and 3 is the maximum value (drawing 3 +1 in a row).
process: I was first contacted for a first round phone interview which consisted of probability questions solely. The second and third rounds were online coding interviews.

question: A man is positioned on one of the vertices of a regular cube. He can travel along any edge to reach the next vertex. He has equal probability to pick any vertex. He wants to reach the diagonally opposite edge of the cube. What is the probability that he will be able to do so?
answer: For the cube probability question, recognize that some vertices are similar with respect to the final destination i.e. there are 3 vertices that are one step away from the end point. and there are 3 vertices that are 2 steps away from the end point. Find the probability of reaching the end point from each of these and then combine the probabilities by multiplying together.
process: First round phone interview with the manager who was a Vice President. More about evaluating the fit. Got a lot of useful information about the teams and their roles within Strats. Great process, very smart folk.

question: The most difficult questions for me were the behavioral questions, I didn't really have the stories prepared to answer them, but what I can say are that none of them were out of left field. answer: For the questions that I don't remember, obviously I don't have an answer. But for the other two, I answered that I worked well under pressure, and I would be careful to check over the work of others and myself when it came to these live situations. I don't really know much about transactions or deals, and it didn't seem pertinent to the role I was applying for so I didn't add much else to that answer. process: Applied via career services. First round interview was with an HR rep. They asked behavioral and fit questions.

question: After applying online and got a response with a month to complete a video interview. I received final round interview. Met 3 people across different assets classes. Overall, very enjoyable with most of the conversation centered around market views.

question: The questions were mostly standard given the research i'd done. I was asked what makes a good salesperson and gave a lengthy answers based on my sales experience. I have been asked this question in other interviews before. I was also asked about the general economy, like what are the implications for the firm of a possible trade war, what risk do I see in the economy. I actually didn't feel too much was 'unexpected' and I had been through a few of these interviews by this stage, and felt prepared. Practice makes perfect!
answer: I think as long as you have a good grasp of the global economy, which would come easily from having a genuine interest, you will be fine. I knew the answers to a lot of the economy questions like rates, and where the housing market was going. Spoke about the possibility of a yield curve inversion and how that could affect markets, of course there is no right answer, as long as you can back up what you say with reason. Answering what makes a good salesperson, I spoke about the importance of listening to clients needs and making sure you tailor the correct solutions. You must also be efficient and always know when to close or push. Essentially as a sales person, if you cannot close a deal you will not generate revenue, so it is is important to be firm sometimes.
process: I was emailed to book in for 1st round phone interviews (i'm in a different city). They were the next day, and consisted of 3X20 minute interviews with 1 person each. Asked general questions about the markets, and then based on my answers, I was asked more probing questions. I was called the night of, and asked to go for final round. Super positive experience with really friendly and knowledgeable interviewers. I was nervous of course, but came out having actually enjoyed the experience. Questions were pretty standard that you would get in any S&T interview, not overly technical.

question: Nothing super unexpected. Be prepared for some very basic questions (like why Markets) at most. question: They asked about my Market Outlook, if I see a market correction coming up. Asked about specific stock prices and if I think they are overvalued or not. Asked about yield curve since I had some fixed income background and how the bond prices would be affected if there was a stock market correction. Asked about specific sectors, and what 3 sectors I would long, and 3 sectors that I would short. They did this with specific stocks as well, where I had to pitch 1 long and 1 short stock. Other questions were economic outlook based - i.e. fed raising interest rates - and how this could affect markets on the whole.
answer: I said the markets might be on track for a correction since specific stocks do show signs of overheating with no quantifiable reasons for growth potential - in this case I talked about Apple and if it is really worth its valuation presently. I also talked about the Fed's planned raising of interest rates 2 more times and how this could affect the economy on the whole. If borrowing becomes more expensive - not only will companies not be able to borrow as much to grow as fast, but a lot of investment management firms will not be able to borrow as much to fund their investments in the FANG stocks - leading to a possible crash in prices.

answer: The most important difference between JPMorgan and other investment banks is that they managed to merge commercial banking and investment banking in a way that made sense. Other companies either failed to do this (Citigroup) or didn't try (Goldman-Sachs and Morgan-Stanley). This meant that you had cultural influences of commercial banking, such as focus on risk, big infrastructure systems, moderation of the "get rich quick" mentality, and a heavily emphasis on process. JPMorgan is also much larger than GS and Morgan-Stanley, which meant more process and more bureaucracy. This can be a bad thing, but when it works, it can be a good thing.

There were also some very easy technical questions: When the yield is lower than coupon rate, is this bond traded at discount or premium? What happens when inflation rises? Would you choose Equity or Bond?

For strength-based questions, I talked about how I worked on my public speaking skills. They were not satisfied with that answer and wanted me to add more. I ended up raising red flag here. For innovative things, I talked about an entrepreneurship competition I have participated in. When the yield is lower, the bond is traded at premium. When inflation, I said Equity because yield should be higher and Bond price should drop. I later realize that equity might not be a great answer here since both assets should be harmed by inflation.

question: For competency questions it is important ot use the STAR method, popular online, to at least provide a framework for your answer. question: The most difficult question was a probability question about the expected value of rolling a die given the chance to roll again. The expected value of rolling a die is 3.5, but if you had the option to roll the die again when would you? What if you had the option to roll the die 2 more times, then in what cases would you roll again? The question was difficult because the 1 on 1 setting made it especially intimidating since you had to walk them through your thought process. I got the same die question asked twice by two different interviewers and got it wrong both times.
answer: I answered the question by first giving the first roll expected value, 3.5. Then, what is the expected value of two rolls? The question is tricky because you have the option, not the obligation, to roll the second time. I said that if you roll a 1, 2 or 3 you would roll again because you were on the low end of the expected value. Then the possibilities become either a 4, 5, or 6 and you stay with that or rolling again with expected value of 3.5. So the average of 3.5, 3.5, 3.5, 4, 5 and 6 is 4.25. So the expected value of the option to roll 1 more time is 4.25. What about option of two more rolls? This time you would only keep a 5 or a 6 in the first roll, since we know the expected value of the 2nd roll is 4.25. Then with the 1, 2, 3 or 4 you would roll again and have the option to roll a third time. So you take the average of 4.25, 4.25, 4.25, 4.25, 5 and 6. The expected value of having the option to roll two more dies is now 4.67.

question: What is multicolinearity. How do you observe and fix the problem.
answer: Multicolinearity is phenomenon in which one predictor variable in a multiple regression model can be linearly predicted from the others with a substantial degree of accuracy. In this situation the coefficient estimates of the multiple regression may change erratically in response to small changes in the model or the data.
