process: I applied to Akuna Capital the Fall of 2017. The first step was online personality test followed by math assessment. After that, there was a one sided online interview that asked more math questions and a couple probability questions.

question: Hnestly, OA was not that difficult. The toughest thing might be to find all the corner solutions for a problem. For example, for a permutation problem, always consider zero '0'. For a problem related to 'year', always consider a lead year. I would say, framing the problem and passing most cases is simple, but passing all the corner cases is a litter bit time-consuming.
answer: For the first two. First frame the question and solve it without considering any corner cases. Passed most of the test cases. Then I spent a lot of time polishing the code to make it fit into corner cases. Not difficult to write, but difficult to focus yourself on considering so many circumstances.
process: kind of long. Maybe I didn't do very well so I waited for about half a month to get feedback for OA. OA consists of three coding problems. Not very difficult but you need to write a lot 'if' 'else' for corner solutions (2/3). The third one requires you to optimize the time. Waiting for the phone screen. Supposed to be technical.

question: The calculation of expected value is not enough for the phone interview. Basically you have to understand what expected value and variance really mean. I was asked why would I want to pay for the expected value of a game in order to play it. And if I am the person who got to decide how much I will pay to play the game, how much will I be willing to pay. I really did not know how to answer... Anyway, the question itself was quite easy: How much would you pay for a dice roll if you are rewarded on the number you roll? What if you can roll again?
answer: The first one, (1+2+3+4+5+6)/6 = 3.5. If I have the chance to roll again, expected payoff will be 0.5*(4+5+6)/3+0.5*3.5 = 4.25. However, with regards to the questions that if I can decide on how much money to play the game, what will my price be? I answered the fair value at first, but the interviewer was not satisfied and asked why do I want to pay at the fair value even if I have the power to decide the price... Weird enough.
process: 1. Math/Sequence 2. Personality 3. Webcam 4. Phone Interview (stopped here) 5. Final Round.

question: Most difficult questions were the sequences. Since there are little resources online to prepare for these questions, it is also even more difficult to succeed on this section. Some sequences were geometric while others were tricky summations that relied on two and even three of the prior terms of the sequence. In addition to numerical sequences, there are letter sequences as well. These usually have a trick or catch that is needed to recognize these. Examples of these are the order of planets in distance from the sun, the first letter of words used to describe order (i.e. first, second, etc.), and months of the year.
answer: The key to these sequences is to try a multitude of different approaches in order to try to figure out the "trick" of the sequence. However, sometimes this is impossible and the pattern or gag will not be immediately or quickly obvious. Thus, it is sometimes necessary to make an educated guess and proceed to the next question. There is no way to skip questions, so if after a while you make no progress it is best to put down a reasonable guess and proceed. For numerical sequences, try to find a element to element pattern, whether it be addition or multiplication, then try to look for a pattern that relies on the previous elements. For letter sequences, see if there is an alphabetical pattern to the sequence, then spend a bit of time trying to think of a creative answer, like the order of the planets above.
process: First round is a mental math and sequence recognition test. Practice with zetamac and tradertest, making sure to be comfortable with order of magnitude manipulation and decimals. Second round is a personality test with around 200 questions similar to MBTI, followed by some simple sequence and logic questiosn. Third round is a short video recorded interview which I am currently waiting for.

question: It started off as basic math questions such as 5 times 5, or 5 minus 9. However, it gradually built up to triple digit multiplication, and division problems. For the sequences start brushing up to answer questions such as "What is the next letter in this sequence: A, C, D, E, ?" You are not allowed to use a calculator at any point, so it is best if you prepare beforehand using any online tests. There are no probability questions or any brainteasers, but definitely expect those going into the second round.
answer: For the alphabetical sequence problems, I entered any random letter since I was not able to prepare for those questions and I wanted to conserve time to answer the maximum number of questions as possible. The key is to try to ace every single problem in the beginning, so you can take more time to think and compute the questions towards the end of the test. Once again, there are no calculators or pen/paper allowed so you have to basically use your previous knowledge regarding mathematics beforehand.
process: First round is a math test. It is comprised of math and arithmetic sequences. You should practice triple digit multiplication and division.

question: First, I was sent a math test. Then I was sent a pattern recognition test. After passing both of these, I was sent an online, one-sided, webcam interview which consists of both behaviorals, such as why trading, why firm, and also simple math questions - probability, brain teasers, mental math, etc. Following the online webcam interview, is a one on one interview with an employee of the firm. In this interview, the employee is mainly testing your analytical abilities, so he/she asks you brain teasers and math questions.
answer: In regards to the online math test and the pattern recognition test, no pen, paper, or calculator are allowed, so I simply answered those questions by doing the mental math in my head and trying to recognize a pattern in my head. In the one sided webcam interview, you can only use paper for one of the questions, so for the first 3 questions, I simply did mental math and answered the behaviorals. For the last question, I used the paper and worked out the math question by writing it out. Be careful, you are only given 1 minute per question to answer, and no time to prepare for any of the questions.
process: I applied through career services and was contacted for a one on one interview with an employee the following week.

question: The interview was not that long maybe 15 minutes but was so hard. Lettered sequences (A,B,C,?)
answer: I read a manual on mental math that I found on amazon. It taught me mental math tricks including how to square numbers and three digit multiplication and division which was not necessary but nice to know for other proprietary trading tests.
process: Took the mental math test online. Mental math wasn’t hard but the sequences were super hard. Failed

question: Making markets on the number of wins of a baseball team during a season. Make sure you know why you are giving the bid and ask that you are giving. The rest of the questions were relatively simple expected value and probability questions. One Monty hall similar type question, a coin flipping question about probability of consecutive heads, and the coin flipping question where you have the chance to flip again if you aren’t happy with the first flip and what is the expected value of that game.
answer: I had trouble with market making questions as I wasn’t sure how it worked at the time but I gave a spread of 5 between bid and ask. For the other questions it’s simple expected value and binomial probability calculations.
process: Math test, Video interview where you record yourself, phone interview with a trader, final round interview with two traders.

question: The most difficult questions were the mathematical questions. The mental maths was extremely tedious and long to do. The sequences were quite unexpected and often had very obscure patterns. Often not involving the alphabet at all but rather abstract concepts (such as the first letter of the months of the years). The phone interview consisted of common brainteasers. The first question was "why trader", but after this, there were no more behavioural questions. The brainteasers ranged from trick questions to questions with a simple trick. there was some conditional probability too.
answer: For the mental maths questions, I had practice beforehand for about a week on online mental maths questions papers. This allowed me to get better and trained with the mental maths questions and allowed me to get better. Sequences were difficult as it is difficult to prepare, but on the test, attempt to find a numerical pattern, if that doesn't work, thinking outside the box will help. For "why trader" have a solid understanding of a trader's job and why that aligns with your interests and skills. Brainteasers can be easily practised with books such as "Heard on the Street". They are usually quite fun to do and often involve a trick which allows them to be solved quickly. None should require more than one or two lines of maths working.
process: Applied online. Got a maths test straight away which involved mental maths questions and also sequences question. Then received a phone interview which tested simple brainteaser questions.

question: The most difficult questions asked were mental math related and probability questions. One question during the phone interview was to compute the square root of a large number. The probability questions were expected value questions. Some coin flipping questions as well. Also, there was a question about put-call parity in the phone interview--given the same conditions and underlying what is worth more a call or put (all else equal). Not too bad in terms of difficulty but really make sure that you explain your thought process.
answer: The mental math questions require practice so I would recommend practicing all sorts of quick math (multiplication, division, addition, subtraction, sq. rt., squares, etc.). Pattern recognition could be practiced by taking a real analysis course or something similar. Probability questions are not difficult but really test your understanding of the fundamentals of probability. For the coin flipping questions you can just use a binomial distribution to solve most of these questions or even other approaches.
process: Mental math and personality test. Online video interview with questions. Phone interview. Superday for the last one.

question: Sequence questions (consisting of number AND letter sequences) and the long division type math questions.
answer: Speed was important but I made sure I took enough time to make sure my answers were not incorrect.
process: 1st round is a 22 minute math test consisting of 7 minutes of mental math questions (with questions like 3960/79) and 15 minutes to do 30 sequence questions. Next round is a personality test with no time limit and some simple logic questions at the end. This is followed by a 5 minute one-sided interview and a web interview.

question: Talk about something you enjoy that isn't academically-related. I wasn't prepared for this one.
answer: Talked about politics for my non-academic interest. It's true but I didn't have an answer prepared, probably should've brought up sports or something else instead.
process: Complete an online mental math/sequence exam. Then you will be sent a personality assessment. After that is a 1-sided web interview (computer asks the questions). Didn't notice at the time but some of the questions are directly out of the "heard on the street" book.

question: The coding challenge comprised of 3 questions and had to finish in 2 hours. I have done a few coding challenges before, prepared for and interviewed with Googled, but this was by far the toughest challenge. The first question was finding the local minima in a 2d array. The other two questions were a regression question on a trade table (which in hindsight was not very difficult) and a path finding algorithm. The path finding question is probably the toughest coding question I have come across. It involved an input array of -1s, 0s and 1s. Starting from the 1s, I was asked to reach another specific 1, avoid the -1s and reach the edge of the matrix. There was also the caveat that once I hit a 0, I had to continue 'sliding' in the same direction. Every person I have asked it to has been as clueless as I was. 2 hours was nowhere near enough to solve all 3.
answer: I solved the local minima question by padding the 2d array with a bunch of max values. Then, I iterated through the 2d array and checked for the neighbor values to identify the local minima. Passed all test cases.
process: Got a hacker rank coding challenge within a couple of days of applying. It comprised of 3 questions and had to finish in 2 hours. Got a hacker rank coding challenge within a couple of days of applying.

question: The phone interview had to be the most difficult. You could easily prepare and study for the parts before this. The hardest question in the phone interview was probably, if you have a rope tied around the circumference of the earth and the circumference of the earth is X then how much rope will you need if you were to life the rope vertically by 1 foot. I dont believe they are looking for the correct answer but seeing if you can think quickly. So explain every step. I didn't do this and I honestly think it hurt me a lot. Explain every single little detail as to why you think it is. Take your time and walk them through your thought process. There was also another question about if a clock falls face down and breaks into 3 different pieces and on each piece the sum of the numbers are the same then what numbers are on each piece of the clock? A little easier. Just add up 1-12. Divide by 3. =26 Then work your way around by adding the largest numbers to the smallest. The answer should be something like 11, 12, 1, and 2. Then 9, 10, 3, and 4. Lastly, 5, 6, 7, 8.
answer: I answered the clock question by simply drawing a picture of a clock to help visualize. Then since I knew the sum of the numbers on each of the faces was equal I added everything up and divided bu 3 for the 3 different broken pieces. After getting 26 I realized the large numbers would offset the small numbers. So I used a little bit of trial and error until I discovered the correct answer. With the rope around the world question I honestly just winged it. I knew a question like this was coming but I honestly didn't know how to answer it so I reccomend just try to think logically and analytically and explain your entire process of arriving to YOUR answer.
process: The process was well laid out. It started with a basic math and sequence test. Followed by a personality test. Then a one sided interview that you recorded and sent to them. After this was the phone interview and if you pass this then you have a day at their office.

question: Tough algorithms questions in the coding interview, given a game with a set of rules, find all valid end states of the game in a given time complexity. Phone interview consists of standard probability questions, nothing too difficult, make sure to understand technical and conceptual aspects of expected values, and be able to do such computations quickly. Know how to answer “options” expected value questions eg how much would you pay for the option to re-roll a dice etc. Brush up on mental math and quick arithmetic techniques.
answer: For preparation, I used Tradertest.com and zetamac.com which helped with quick mental math. For the coding interview, the usual books and websites are good ie Cracking the Coding Interview and HackerRank/Leetcode. Books with probability puzzles are also useful in preparing for the phone interview. Maybe review a probability textbook as well to make sure you have he key concepts at your fingertips. There usually is no crazy trick to answering the questions, they are designed to make sure you have an extremely good handle on the fundamentals, and not necessarily a great deal of experience in advanced topics.
process: Pleasant and professional process - starts off with a mental math and sequences test and possibly a coding test if applying for quant position, then personality assessment, then phone interview with a trader, then final on site.

question: The mental math is wuite tricky, needs practice. Sequences aswell, needs fair bit of practice. The personaility test, I just answered how i would regularly, didnt not try to skew my answers a certain way. For the hirevue, i found the interface confusing, the first behavioral was just about your outside interests. But the second question consisting of a bunch lf mental math was confusing. The interface wouldnt let me scroll down to view all the questions, so i ended up only answering one of the listed mental math. The next two are probability questions, think coinflips/die/cubes etc.
answer: The behavioral is just like any other. I just talked about my outside interests, had 1 min for this. The mental math i said outloud which one i was answering and answered (lol), would have been better if there was an option to skip or something since u only have a minute and a bunch are listed, and my scrolling interface wasnt working. The probability was something about probability of getting all heads in three flips, given that the first one is heads, i just used bayes theoream and got my answer to be 1/7.
process: Fairly straight foward, as described on website. First round is mental math nd sequences, second is personality test. Third is hirevue, with one behavioural and 3 math. Finished this third stage so far

question: Starts out with easy probability questions (rolling dice expected pay, etc)
answer: Just build out the knowledge for probabilities, (Bayes, etc) and be familiar to answer questions related to it on the mindset.
process: Math test > Personality Test (Go for INTJ) > Webcam Hirevue (I received it this year but not last year) > Phone Interview with senior trader > Superday at Chicago

question: Haven't done the video interview yet, but here are some possible behavioral questions: what's the biggest risk you have ever taken? What qualities does a market maker need to have? Do you have these qualities? Why are you interested in trading? Tell us about one extracurricular activity you do.
answer: mental math: 1) **M**arch, **A**pril, **M**ay, **J**une, **J**uly, **A**ugust 2) Every minute the hour hand moves 360/12/60 = 0.5, the minute hand moves 360/60 = 6, at 3 pm the hour hand is 90, so 90+0.5x=6x, 180+x=12x, x=180/11=16.3636, 0.3636*60 = 22, so in 18min and 22 seconds will the hour and minute hand overlap.
process: 5 rounds in total: 1) Mental Math Test ( arithmetic + sequence ) 2) Personality Test (185 questions) 3) Video Interview (4 min) 4) Phone Interview (about 30 min) 5) Onsite

question: There was a question on the webcam interview that asked about a 10×10×10 cube made up off 1000 1×1×1 cubes. They ask you to remove the outer layer and inform them of how many blocks you have removed. I believe this question wants to see if you can give a range like you would in trading options. I answered around 300-400 cubes for I wasn't sure and only had 45 seconds to answer if I remember correctly maybe a minute.
answer: As explained before, for the cube question I just gave a range I thought the number fell in. I honestly didn't know the answer on the spot and didn't have the time to calculate it. For the personality section (the second stage of the interview process) I went to 16personalities and practiced until I got the INTJ personality. I wouldn't recommend this but if you really want the job this is the best personality to follow. Then for the webcam I practiced my basic math and probabilty skills. Probability questions can ask about expected value, probability of getting 3 heads on 3 coin tosses if the first one was heads (there is a theorem for this I just can't remember) and other simple probabilty games. I'm getting ready to move onto the phone interview but again I hear they ask probability questions and some behavior questions along with option basics.
process: This is a 5 step process.

question: You have a 3 x 3 x 3 cube. You paint the outside of the cube then break it into smaller cubes (27 total) you pick a cube at random and then toss it. What is the probability that it lands painted side up?
answer: I mostly prepared for these via online forums.
process: I interviewed for the Junior Trader Role at Akuna Capital. The first round was a math test consisting of questions on mental math and sequences & series. The following round was a personality test which was then followed by a 5 minute video interview. The video interview was similar to the math test where you were shown numbers (written out in words) on the screen and had to answer as many as possible within the minute. There were also 2 probability questions which you had to solve under a minute. The next step was the phone interview with a trader. This consisted of mostly probability and statistics questions such as dice questions.

question: Unfortunately a lot of the questions asked are not supposed to be given out as it would unfairly help interviewees with access, however, I can give some example problems that are common to the. types they gave or those that they gave which are common enough to find online with enough care. Mostly probability questions or brainteasers, which can be hard if you don't have the requisite knowledge, but have correct answers. The hardest question I was asked was more broad and had no correct answer. On the super day, one trader asked me if I were to give you $10 million today and ask for it back tomorrow, what would you do? How would that change if I said 6 months? 3 years? I found this to be pretty difficult, especially since at the time I was great with math, but had no prior knowledge of money management and trading.
answer: I offered a few low risk strategies like investing in bonds or in the S and P 500. It was difficult to say if they thought my answers were poor. I didn't know well at the time what they expected, and to be honest still do not really understand what they were hoping for from a college sophomore. Just make sure whatever answer you do give you are confident with it, and be careful about making any guarantees and be ready for the math to follow. For example, I offered a yearly rate of return on one strategy, and the trader asked how long would it take to double, and also in the time frame (3 years) how much would the money compound. Not totally difficult but mental math can be troublesome in stressful interviews.
process: First they send a math IQ assessment, mostly mental math and pattern recognition, 80 questions in 8 min. Next, if you score well enough, you take a personality test to see if you are fit for the industry. Once you pass that, it is an automated video interview where they record you answering mental math, brainteasers, probability and stat questions. After that it was a phone interview with similar type technical questions. I was off site so the final super day was Skype interview with 3 traders, one option focused, one value focused, one math focused.

question: Even though I was warned about the sequences questions, I was still dumbfounded by how ridiculously hard some of them were. answer: Let's consider first what happens if the barrel is spun after the first shot is fired. In this case, any one of the chambers is equally likely to end up in the firing position. Since four of the six chambers are empty, this means the probability of not getting shot is 4/6, or 2/3. On the other hand, if the barrel is not spun, the only way the gun will fire is if the empty chamber from the first time the trigger is pulled is replaced by a chamber with a bull. we see the probability of not getting shot if the chamber is not spun is 3/4. Since this is larger than 2/3, you are better off not spinning the chamber before the trigger is pulled again.

answer: One good way to do this problem is to have three categories: only one eight, two eights, and three eights. For the first one, choose one digit from the three as eight, the rest can be any number except eight, that is nine different choices for the other two digits. The following two other cases are similar. Remember to multiply the times eight appears. The final answer should be: 1*3C1*9*9+2*3C2*9+3*3C3=243+54+3=300. I did not multiply the times at first and chose to use another solution for my second calculation, which leaded to a failure.

question: You have 27 race horses. You can race five of them at a time. You don't know what each one's time even if you race them (you only know the order in which the five horses raced ended up in). How many races do you need to make, in what order, with what horses, in order to know the top three horses overall from the pool of 27 horses? You also need to know not just which three horses these are, but their order relative to each other (who came first, second, third). Optimize your strategy to find the minimum number of races.
answer: I just tried it out and went through it. You can observe that 27//5 = 5 with a remainder of two. Leave two horses aside and then race five groups of five horses. Then race the leaders of those five groups in a race. answer: For Fibonacci sequence, I just use a matrix representation of the two equations F(n) = F(n-1)+F(n-2) and F(n-1) = F(n-1). Then I calculate the n-th power of the matrix to get an expression for F(n) in terms of the matrix. question: For two basketball players player A and player B, it player A has higher shooting average in both the first half of the game and second half of the game than player B, is it possible for player B to have higher shooting average in the entire game?
answer: There is a way for player B to have higher shooting average than player A if we think of the entire game. For example, if player A made 100 shot in the first half and scored 1, while player B made 1 shot in the first half and missed it, A has higher shooting average than B. Each turn, a player has the option to draw between 1 and 5 cards from the deck. The player who draws the last card wins.If 5 six-sided dice are thrown, what is the probability that the same number is rolled by exactly 3 dice? Given a box, calculate the minimum distance between two furthest corners. Imagine you have a lottery with 100,000 tickets. There is one ticket among the 100,000 that pays of $100,000. There are 5 tickets that pay $12,500 and 10 tickets that pay $1,000. What is the fair price (expected value..) of this game? Has to be done in your head.
answer: Divided the group of balls into 3-3-2. Weighed the groups of 3 against eachother. In the case where they are equal, weigh the group of 2 balls to determine which is heavier. If one group is heavier, weigh 2 arbitrary balls from the heavy group. If they are equal, it is the 3rd ball from that group. Otherwise, it is the heavier ball. If you are picking where there are 7-11 cards left, you will win because you can draw the appropriate number of cards to force your opponent to draw 1-5 cards from 6 cards, allowing you to grab the last card.

How do you measure exactly 45 minutes using these two pieces of string and a lighter? The other difficult questions were on the math tests that they gave on-site. The questions weren't too hard, but you didn't have a lot of time so you had to be very fast in doing the math. As for the behavioral questions, they were all pretty standard.
answer: For the string question, you first have to identify that if you burn a piece of string from both sides at the same time, then it will burn out in exactly 30 minutes. So you start burning one string from both sides while starting to burn the other string from one side. After 30 minutes, the string burning from both sides will disappear, and the string burning from one side will have 30 minutes to go. Now you burn the remaining string from both sides. After 15 more minutes, that string will disappear. In total, 30+15=45 minutes will have passed.

question: Suppose there are eight balls, one of which is lighter than the others. Given a judge's scale, how many weighings are necessary to determine which ball is the odd one out and how?
answer: Two weighings are necessary. Split the balls into groups as follows: 3-3-2. Compare the two 3-groups. If one weighs less than the other, then the light ball is in the lighter 3-group. In this case, compare two arbitrary balls in that 3-group. If one weighs less than the other clearly that is the light ball. Otherwise, the third ball is the light ball. In the case that the two 3-groups weigh the same, compare the two balls in the 2-group. Whichever weighs less is the light ball.

question: Brainteaser: You have two opaque jars and 50 blue marbles and 50 red marbles. You can choose how to divide the marbles into each jar. You must maximize the probability of picking a single blue marble assuming you can't see/don't know which marbles are in which jar. They gave me plenty of time to think about the question and we're really nice about the process, so it wasn't too bad at all in reality. I actually enjoyed thinking through many of their brainteasers, but this was the first S&T interview where I really got many.
answer: I walked them through my thought process. First I thought the obvious answer was put all the blue marbles in one jar and put all the red marbles in the other jar thereby ensuring a 50-50 probability of choosing a blue marble. But then if you go to the other extreme, you can put all the of the marbles in one jar and none in the other. Then if you take out one blue and put it in one jar, and put the rest in the other, you have at least a half chance of selecting blue just by randomly selecting that jar. Then you have approximately a quarter chance of choosing blue if you select the other jar. I got it right, but they really appreciated me walking them through the process.

question: From a deck of 52 cards pick 26 at random. From this set of 26 you pick two cards. You win if the both of these cards are of the same color. Is this a game you would prefer over one in which you win by picking two (first two picks) of the same color at random from a deck of 26 with equal number of black and red
answer: One way to argue if the 26 random cards are even, then its the same as the 2nd situation, but if its uneven (12R 14B), then probability is 12/26 * 11/25 + 14/26 * 13/25 > the probability of the 2nd option. And the probability just gets better as the draw is more skewed.

question: What is the payoff structure of different kind of equity derivatives products including, options, warrants, ELS, ELN, turbo warrants? What is the methodology for index rebalancing? What is the adjustment for equity derivative products for corporate action? What is the P&L impact of the derivative products when the underlying moves? Basically, they asked a bunch of different technical question regarding you knowledge on equity derivatives so that make sure you understand the structure, risk and payoff of the most commonly traded derivatives?
answer: For payoff of the derivative products, it is generally the combination of options and fixed coupon. So you just have to breakdown the structure of the derivative products and add the payoff of all the products which will give the total payoff. Make sure you understand not only basic options but also exotic options such as Knock-in/Knock-out kind of options. Also, understand the Greek of different options and how they impact the risk of the total portfolio. For the corporate action, options will normally be adjusted on strike price and entitlement ratio.

question: Interviewer asked for a lot of specifics about previous client coverage, even down to names of companies.
